misconceptions.believed: The profiler failing to classify class names was a plain omission, fixed by one line adding them to the same histogram as everything else.
misconceptions.revealed_by: Writing that line and looking at the result. PascalCase jumped to a large share and became meaningless: it now mixed correctly named classes with functions named the Java way, which are opposite verdicts wearing the same token shape.
misconceptions.corrected_to: The omission was avoiding a real conflation, badly. Conformance is judged per identifier kind, which keeps both signals; the display changed too, because NAMING showing PascalCase 0% above 'classes are PascalCase 100%' is a contradiction on screen even when both numbers are right.
misconceptions.generalisable_lesson: The one-line fix passed every test that existed and would have shipped a worse metric than the bug it fixed.

misconceptions.believed: The enhancement was done when the detectors worked. The engine reads other people's codebases; it is not a judge of this one.
misconceptions.revealed_by: Running it on vibecoder/ and reading the output. Max complexity had gone from 39 to 73, and the worst function in the codebase by a factor of two was _analyse_tree - the function just doubled in size with a twenty-branch elif chain.
misconceptions.corrected_to: Replaced the chain with a dispatch table keyed on node type. Max complexity fell to 29 and max nesting from 5 to 4, guarded by a test that every original detector still fires.
misconceptions.generalisable_lesson: A profiler whose own report condemns it is not one to trust. Running the tool on the tool is close to free and was the most useful twenty minutes in the session.

misconceptions.believed: The first nesting implementation reporting a maximum depth of 22 was a real finding about some horrible function.
misconceptions.revealed_by: Looking for the function. It was _analyse_tree again, whose elif chain is one level to a reader: each elif is an If inside the previous one's orelse, so an AST walk sees a 22-deep staircase where a person sees a flat list.
misconceptions.corrected_to: Nesting is measured over statements rather than by walking the tree, and an elif chain counts once. The metric is about the indentation a person looks at, so the AST shape is the wrong thing to count.
misconceptions.generalisable_lesson: The number was absurd enough to check. A plausible wrong number - 4 instead of 3 - would have shipped unexamined.

decisions.decision: Conventions are counted per identifier kind
decisions.rationale: The same token shape is a correct class and an incorrect function; one number cannot say which.

decisions.decision: A kind with no instances is absent rather than 0%
decisions.rationale: 'You name every class wrongly' is a bad thing to tell somebody who has written no classes.

decisions.decision: Nesting is a statement walk and an elif chain counts once
decisions.rationale: The metric is about the indentation a person sees, and the AST disagrees with the screen exactly here.

decisions.decision: Complexity is reported as median, p90 and max
decisions.rationale: Max is one function on a bad day; the distribution describes the codebase.
Its own metrics condemned the chain. A table is flat, and adding a detector no longer adds a branch.

decisions.decision: Detectors are narrow rather than eager
decisions.rationale: A profile is read as fact. x % 7 is not string formatting and logger.format() is not str.format.

decisions.decision: The signature describes style, never quality
decisions.rationale: The profiler exists so the game can meet somebody where they are; a report that reads as a scolding stops being run.

friction.description: Test file names cannot be keyword arguments: self.profile(a_py=...) writes a file called a_py, which the *.py globber never finds, so every assertion silently measured an empty directory and thirty-five tests failed at once. The existing suite used **{'a.py': ...} and I did not look first. Added a one() helper to the base class.
style_signature labels are joined with / for display and two contained commas, which read as extra traits. Caught by a test written for the purpose rather than by eye.

open_questions.question: VibeVector gained six fields. from_json drops unknown keys and new fields have defaults, so old profiles still load - but a profile written today and read by an older build silently loses signals. Is that the migration story T2 W7 wants, or does the vector need a version?

The signature thresholds were chosen by profiling five stdlib packages and this repository. That is six data points. Do they hold on real application code, and how would we know without collecting profiles we have promised never to collect?

_record_constants only judges module-level assignments, so a class-level constant is not counted. A codebase keeping constants on classes gets a conformance ratio built from very few names. Should the sample size be reported next to the ratio?

Six of the new patterns map to no tag, so they enrich the display and cannot influence level selection. Is that the right split, or should walrus and match_statement recommend a 'modern Python' level that does not exist yet?
